title: Choosing your needle for cross-stitch
subtitle: The right tapestry needle size for each fabric count
excerpt: Cross-stitch uses the tapestry needle: a blunt-tipped needle that slips between fabric threads rather than piercing them. The size number is counter-intuitive: higher numbers are smaller needles. Size 24 is the standard for 14-count Aida. The right needle slips through Aida holes with minimal resistance.
sourceNotes: Needle sizing conventions documented in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. The blunt tapestry needle standard for counted cross-stitch is universal.

content.text: specific needle: the tapestry needle, which has a blunt tip. The blunt tip slips through the holes in the Aida weave without splitting the woven threads. A sharp embroidery needle pierces the threads rather than the holes and makes the fabric harder to read.

Tapestry needle sizes are numbered counterintuitively: larger numbers are smaller needles. Size 22 is larger than size 28. The needle should pass through the Aida holes with minimal resistance: too large and it distorts the holes; too small and it slips through and the thread bunches.
The largest holes take the largest standard cross-stitch needle. Use three strands of floss.
The standard beginner combination. Use two strands of floss for the fill and one strand for the back-stitch outline.
16-count Aida or 28-count evenweave: size 26 tapestry needle.
A slightly finer needle for a slightly finer fabric. Two strands still work at 16-count.
18-count Aida or 32-count linen: size 28 tapestry needle.
Fine detail work. One strand of floss at this count. A magnifier is useful.

Tapestry needles develop a slight burr with use and eventually drag on the thread rather than pulling cleanly through the holes. Run a needle through an emery strawberry (the small pin cushion attachment on some needle books) to smooth the surface. Replace needles when they start to feel rough or bent.
